title: Beef kaldereta
intro: Beef braised until tender in a thick, spicy tomato sauce enriched with liver spread and melted cheese, with potatoes, carrots, bell peppers and olives. It is rich and savory, and the dish people make when there are guests coming.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef on all sides in batches. Set aside.
Lower the heat to medium. Sauté the onion in the same pot until soft, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for a minute. Return the beef and its juices, then add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the beef is fork-tender, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if the sauce gets too thick.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until just tender.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies and simmer until the sauce turns thick and glossy.
Add the bell peppers, olives and cheese. Cook until the cheese melts and the peppers are bright but still a little crisp.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper. Remove the bay leaves and serve hot with rice.

tips: For potatoes and carrots that hold their shape, fry them in the oil until lightly browned before the beef goes in, set them aside, and add them back for the last 10 minutes.

title: Beef kaldereta with peanut butter
intro: Beef kaldereta with creamy peanut butter stirred into the tomato sauce in place of liver spread, so the sauce turns thick, nutty and slightly sweet. A good choice when someone at the table does not care for the taste of liver.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef on all sides in batches. Set aside.
Lower the heat to medium and sauté the onion until soft. Add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Return the beef and its juices to the pot. Add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the beef is tender, stirring now and then and adding water if the pot gets dry.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.

In a small bowl, whisk the peanut butter with a ladle of the hot sauce until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the chilies. Simmer until the sauce thickens, stirring so it does not catch on the bottom.
Add the bell pepper and peas and cook until the peas are heated through.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper, remove the bay leaves and serve with rice.

tips: Peanut butter scorches easily once it is in the sauce, so keep the heat low and stir from the bottom of the pot. Natural unsweetened peanut butter works too; add 1 tsp sugar if you use it.

title: Kalderetang kambing
intro: Goat meat braised until tender in a spicy tomato sauce thickened with mashed liver, with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers. It is rich, peppery and a little gamey, and a favorite for parties and pulutan.

steps.text: Toss the goat with the vinegar and salt in a bowl and let it stand to tame the gamey smell.
Drain, rinse the meat under cold water and pat it dry.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the goat in batches. Set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until soft, then add the tomatoes and cook until they break down.
Return the goat with the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the meat is tender, adding water as needed.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Stir in the liver and chilies. Simmer, pressing some of the liver against the side of the pot so it melts into the sauce and thickens it.
Add the bell pepper and olives and cook until the pepper softens slightly.
Season with fish sauce and plenty of black pepper. Serve hot.

tips: Goat varies a lot: young goat can be tender in an hour, older goat may need 2 hours or more. A pressure cooker brings the braise down to about 35 minutes. No fresh liver? Use a small can (85 g) of liver spread.

title: Chicken kaldereta
intro: Chicken simmered in a spicy tomato sauce with liver spread, potatoes, carrots and melted cheese. It has the richness of beef kaldereta and is ready in under an hour.

steps.text: Pat the chicken dry and season lightly with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat and brown the chicken skin side down. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until soft.
Return the chicken and add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes and carrots, cover and simmer until the chicken is cooked through and the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce thickens.
Add the bell pepper, peas and cheese and stir until the cheese melts into the sauce.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Thighs and drumsticks stay juicy through the simmer; breast meat dries out. If you only have breast, add it after the potatoes have cooked for 5 minutes.

title: Pork kaldereta
intro: Cubes of pork shoulder braised in tomato sauce with liver spread, potatoes, carrots and green peas until the sauce is thick and spicy. It cooks faster than beef kaldereta, and the pork fat gives the sauce a silky finish.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add the pork and cook, stirring now and then, until lightly browned and some fat has rendered.
Push the pork to one side and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies and simmer until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
Add the bell peppers and peas and cook until the peppers soften slightly.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve hot.

tips: Pork kaldereta tastes even better the next day. Reheat it with a splash of water, since the liver spread thickens the sauce as it cools.

title: Oxtail kaldereta
intro: Oxtail braised slowly until the meat slips off the bone, then finished in a spicy kaldereta sauce with liver spread, cheese and vegetables. The collagen from the oxtail makes the sauce sticky and deeply savory.

steps.text: Put the oxtail in a large pot, cover with water and bring to a boil. Boil to release the scum, then drain and rinse the pieces and the pot.
Pat the oxtail dry. Heat the oil in the clean pot over medium-high heat and brown the pieces on all sides in batches. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until soft. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for a minute.
Return the oxtail with the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently until the meat pulls away from the bone, adding water if needed.
Spoon off as much fat from the surface as you can.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies, then the bell peppers and cheese. Simmer until the cheese melts and the sauce is thick.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Make the braise a day ahead and chill it overnight: the fat sets on top and lifts off in one piece. A pressure cooker gets oxtail tender in about 50 minutes.

title: Chicken afritada
intro: Chicken simmered in a mild tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots, bell peppers and green peas. It is lighter than kaldereta, with no liver spread or cheese, and an easy weekday ulam.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Fry the potatoes and carrots until the edges are lightly browned, then set aside.
In the same oil, brown the chicken on both sides over medium-high heat.
Add the onion and garlic and cook until the onion softens.
Pour in the fish sauce and let it sizzle for a minute, then add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer.
Return the potatoes and carrots and simmer until the chicken is cooked through and the vegetables are tender.
Add the bell peppers and peas and cook until the peppers are just tender.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Frying the potatoes and carrots first keeps them from breaking up in the sauce and brings out their sweetness.

title: Pork afritada
intro: Pork cubes braised in tomato sauce until tender, with potatoes, carrots, bell pepper and peas. The sauce is mild, savory and slightly sweet, and it goes a long way over rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the pork and cook, stirring, until it changes color and some fat renders.
Add the fish sauce and cook for 2 minutes, then pour in the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has thickened.
Add the bell pepper and peas and cook a few minutes more.
Taste and adjust with salt, pepper and the sugar if the sauce is too sharp. Serve hot.

tips: Pork shoulder with a little fat stays tender; very lean cuts turn dry and stringy in the long simmer.

title: Chicken afritada with hotdogs
intro: A sweeter afritada with sliced red hotdogs simmered alongside the chicken, potatoes and carrots. Kids tend to go for the hotdogs first, and it often shows up at birthday parties.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and fry the hotdogs until they blister. Set aside.
Brown the chicken in the same oil, then add the onion and garlic and cook until soft.
Add the fish sauce, tomato sauce, water and sugar. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes, carrots and hotdogs and simmer until the chicken is cooked through and the potatoes are tender.
Add the bell pepper and peas and simmer until the sauce is thick.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Banana ketchup in place of the sugar is a common shortcut: use 2 tbsp and cut the tomato sauce by the same amount.

title: Beef afritada
intro: Beef braised low and slow in a tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots, peas and bell pepper. It is the plainer cousin of kaldereta: mild and comforting, with no liver spread, cheese or chili.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper and brown it in the oil over medium-high heat in batches. Set aside.
Sauté the onion, garlic and tomatoes in the same pot until the tomatoes are soft.
Return the beef, add the fish sauce, tomato sauce, water and bay leaves and bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer until the beef is tender, adding water if the sauce reduces too much.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Add the bell pepper and peas and cook until heated through.
Season with salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Chuck, brisket or shank all work. Avoid lean sirloin, which stays tough no matter how long it simmers.

title: Beef mechado
intro: Thick chunks of beef threaded with strips of pork fat, marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, then braised in tomato sauce with potatoes. The fat melts into the meat as it cooks, and the sauce is tangy and savory.

steps.text: With a thin knife, poke a deep slit through each chunk of beef and push a strip of pork fat into it.
Put the beef in a bowl with the soy sauce, calamansi juice and a good grind of pepper and marinate.
Lift the beef out and reserve the marinade. Pat the beef dry and brown it on all sides in the oil over medium-high heat. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until soft.
Return the beef with the reserved marinade, tomato sauce, water and bay leaves and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the beef is tender, turning the chunks now and then.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Add the bell pepper and sugar and simmer until the sauce thickens.
Taste for salt and pepper. Slice the chunks thickly if they are large and serve with plenty of sauce.

tips: Pork back fat is sold at the pork stall in most wet markets. If you skip the larding, use a well-marbled cut like chuck or brisket so the beef stays moist.

title: Pork mechado
intro: Pork belly cubes marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, then braised in tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots and red bell pepper. The sauce is salty, tangy and rich from the rendered pork fat.

steps.text: Combine the pork, soy sauce, calamansi juice and a good grind of pepper and marinate.
Lift the pork out and reserve the marinade. Brown the pork in the oil over medium-high heat until the fat starts to render.
Add the onion and garlic and cook until soft.
Pour in the reserved marinade, tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Add the bell pepper and sugar and simmer until the sauce is thick.
Taste for salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: If too much fat pools on top, spoon some off before adding the potatoes. Pork shoulder (kasim) works for a leaner version; add 10 minutes to the simmer.

title: Chicken mechado
intro: Chicken marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, then simmered in tomato sauce with bay leaves, potatoes and carrots. It has the tangy, soy-rich sauce of beef mechado and is ready in under an hour.

steps.text: Toss the chicken with the soy sauce, calamansi juice and some pepper and marinate.
Lift the chicken out, reserving the marinade, and brown it in the oil over medium-high heat. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until soft.
Return the chicken with the marinade, tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer until the chicken is cooked through and the vegetables are tender.
Add the bell pepper and simmer until the sauce thickens.
Taste for salt and pepper and serve.

tips: The soy marinade already salts the chicken, so taste before adding any salt at the end.

title: Pork menudo
intro: Small cubes of pork, potatoes, carrots and hotdogs simmered in tomato sauce and finished with raisins and red bell pepper. It is savory with little sweet bursts from the raisins, and a fixture at fiestas and family gatherings.

steps.text: Mix the pork with the soy sauce and calamansi juice and marinate.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the pork with its marinade and cook, stirring, until the pork is no longer pink.
Add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes, carrots and hotdogs and simmer, uncovered, until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the bell pepper and raisins and cook until the sauce is thick.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Cut everything about the same small size so each spoonful gets a bit of everything and the potatoes cook in time with the pork.

title: Pork and liver menudo
intro: The classic menudo of diced pork and pork liver with potatoes, carrots and chickpeas in tomato sauce. The liver goes in at the end so it stays tender and gives the sauce a deep, savory flavor.

steps.text: Mix the pork with the soy sauce and calamansi juice and marinate.
Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a pot over high heat and sear the liver for about a minute, just until it browns outside. Set aside.
Add the rest of the oil and sauté the onion, garlic and tomatoes until the tomatoes soften.
Add the pork with its marinade and cook until it is no longer pink.
Pour in the tomato sauce and water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes, carrots and chickpeas and simmer, uncovered, until the potatoes are tender.
Return the liver with the bell pepper and raisins and simmer just until the liver is cooked through.
Season with fish sauce and pepper and serve.

tips: Liver turns grainy and tough when overcooked. Sear it quickly at the start and add it back only for the last few minutes.

title: Waknatoy
intro: A menudo-style stew of pork, pork liver, potatoes and green peas finished with sweet pickle relish. The relish gives the tomato sauce a sweet and tangy edge that sets it apart from regular menudo.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a pot over high heat and sear the liver until browned outside. Set aside.
Add the rest of the oil and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the pork and cook, stirring, until lightly browned. Add the soy sauce and cook for a minute.
Pour in the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Return the liver with the bell pepper, peas and pickle relish and simmer until the liver is just cooked.
Season with fish sauce, a pinch of sugar if needed, and pepper. Serve with rice.

tips: Add the relish near the end so it keeps its tang. Taste before adding sugar, since some relish brands are quite sweet.

title: Chicken menudo
intro: Diced chicken and chicken liver cooked menudo-style with potatoes, carrots, raisins and bell pepper in tomato sauce. It is quicker than pork menudo and a little lighter.

steps.text: Mix the chicken with the soy sauce and calamansi juice and marinate.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the chicken with its marinade and cook until the pieces turn opaque.
Add the tomato sauce, water, potatoes and carrots. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the chicken livers and simmer until they are cooked through but still soft.
Add the bell pepper and raisins and cook until the sauce is thick.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Skip the livers if your family does not like them and add an extra potato instead.

title: Pork pochero
intro: Pork simmered in a light tomato broth with saba bananas, sweet potato, chickpeas, cabbage and bok choy, with a garlicky eggplant sauce on the side. It is sweet, savory and filling, and a favorite Sunday or holiday meal.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat and fry the saba until golden on both sides. Set aside.
Brown the pork in the same pot, then add the onion, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the tomatoes soften.
Add the fish sauce, tomato sauce and water. Bring to a boil and skim, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the sweet potato, chickpeas, pork and beans and chorizo and simmer until the sweet potato is tender.
Add the green beans and cabbage and simmer until just tender.
Add the bok choy and fried saba and cook until the bok choy wilts.
For the sauce, grill or broil the eggplants until the skins are charred and the flesh is soft. Peel, then mash the flesh with the garlic, vinegar, sugar, salt and pepper.
Season the pochero with salt and pepper and serve with the eggplant sauce on the side.

tips: Choose saba that is yellow with a few black spots: ripe enough to be sweet, firm enough to hold together in the broth.

title: Beef pochero
intro: Beef brisket simmered until tender in a tomato broth with fried saba bananas, potatoes, green beans, cabbage and chickpeas. The bananas sweeten the broth, which is spooned generously over rice.

steps.text: Put the beef, water, quartered onion and peppercorns in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim off the scum.
Cover and simmer until the beef is tender.
Lift out the beef and keep 5 cups of the broth.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the saba until golden on both sides. Set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the chopped onion, garlic and tomatoes until soft. Add the fish sauce and tomato sauce.
Add the beef and reserved broth and bring to a boil. Add the potatoes and chickpeas and simmer until the potatoes are tender.
Add the green beans and cabbage and simmer until just tender.
Return the saba, season with salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Boil the beef a day ahead and chill the broth. The fat sets on top and is easy to lift off, which keeps the finished pochero clean-tasting.

title: Chicken pochero
intro: A quicker pochero of chicken, chorizo de Bilbao, potatoes and fried saba in a tomato broth with cabbage and bok choy. It has the sweet and savory balance of the pork version in about an hour.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat and fry the saba until golden. Set aside. Fry the chorizo for a minute and set it aside too.
Brown the chicken in the same pot, then add the onion, garlic and tomatoes and cook until soft.
Add the fish sauce, tomato sauce and water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes, chorizo and pork and beans and simmer until the potatoes are tender.
Add the cabbage and simmer until it starts to soften.
Add the bok choy and saba and cook until the bok choy wilts.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Chorizo de Bilbao is salty, so hold back on the fish sauce until you taste the broth at the end.

title: Pork estofado
intro: Pork belly braised in soy sauce, vinegar and brown sugar until sweet, tangy and sticky, then finished with carrots and fried saba bananas. It is richer and sweeter than adobo.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and fry the saba until golden on both sides. Set aside.
Brown the pork in the same oil, then add the garlic and onion and cook until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, brown sugar, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring so the sharp edge cooks off.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has reduced.
Add the fried saba and simmer until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Taste and adjust with more sugar or soy sauce, then serve with rice.

tips: Fry the saba until it is deep golden so it holds together, and add it only at the end; it turns mushy if it simmers long.

title: Pata estofado
intro: Pork hock simmered until gelatinous, then braised in soy sauce, vinegar and brown sugar with fried saba bananas. The sauce turns thick and glossy, and the skin is soft enough to cut with a spoon.

steps.text: Put the pata, water, peppercorns and bay leaves in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim, then cover and simmer until the skin is soft.
Lift out the pata and keep 2 cups of the broth.
Heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the saba until golden on both sides. Set aside.
Sauté the garlic and onion in the same pot until fragrant. Add the pata, soy sauce, brown sugar and reserved broth and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer, turning the pieces now and then, until the meat is very tender.
Stir in the cornstarch mixture and simmer until the sauce thickens.
Add the saba, taste for salt and pepper and serve.

tips: A pressure cooker cuts the boiling time to about 35 minutes. Ask the butcher to cut the pata into rings for you; it takes a heavy cleaver.

title: Chicken estofado
intro: Chicken braised in soy sauce, vinegar and brown sugar with carrots and fried saba bananas. The sauce is sweet and tangy, a little like a sweeter adobo, and very good over rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and fry the saba until golden. Set aside.
Brown the chicken in the same oil, then add the onion and garlic and cook until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, brown sugar, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the chicken is almost cooked through.
Add the carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has reduced.
Add the saba and simmer until the sauce is glossy.
Taste and adjust with sugar or soy sauce, then serve.

tips: Bone-in thighs give the best sauce. Boneless thighs cook faster: cut the covered simmer to 12 minutes.
